title: Raasta
kicker: The most scenic walk in Philadelphia, not the fastest one.
role: TODO: Concept, cartography, route engine and front end (solo, for the Wharton Generative AI Studio?)
data: City street centerlines and High Injury Network
OpenDataPhilly parks, hydrology, art and historic districts
intro: Raasta finds the most scenic walk in Philadelphia, not the fastest one. You say how you feel, or what kind of walk you want, pick how many extra minutes you can spare, and it builds a real route around that, then narrates it as you go.

Underneath is a Python engine that scores all 196,411 walkable segments in the city: 151,726 street trees, the 2015 tree canopy, parks, water, public art, historic districts, a noise model and the High Injury Network. A language model reads your mood into a recipe that re-weights what is attractive. It never picks the streets, and nothing can switch off what is dangerous.

From City Hall to Rittenhouse Square the fastest walk is 14 minutes. Raasta's takes 22, spends 8 of them on nicer streets, and passes the City Hall fountain, the Rittenhouse-Fitler historic district and the Church of the Holy Trinity. The route draws on a 3D Mapbox map with comic-bubble callouts written from the real things it passes.

title: The Cloud Has a Footprint
kicker: US data centers and AI campuses, mapped against water stress.
data: IM3 Open Source Data Center Atlas (PNNL), derived from OpenStreetMap
intro: Two interactive maps of the physical side of AI. The first puts 1,472 existing US data centers on the map alongside 34 new AI campuses that are already running and 43 more that are coming. The second lays the same campuses over the basins where water is already scarce.

39% of the new AI campuses sit in those basins. The maps are built in Python from the IM3 Data Center Atlas, Epoch AI's Frontier Data Centers list and WRI Aqueduct 4.0, and published as Mapbox pages with a floating card, hover details and a legend that toggles each layer.
They are the first two studies in a series called The Cloud Has a Footprint. What AI Burns and Where AI Is at Risk come next.

title: 30 Day Map Challenge
kicker: Seven static maps in seven days, from one shared Python toolkit.
location: Big Sur, San Francisco, New York, Philadelphia, Mumbai
data: City of Philadelphia footprints, parks and heat vulnerability
British Library 1843 map via Wikimedia Commons
intro: Seven maps in seven days for the 30 Day Map Challenge, each one a question about a city answered with a number. 12 towers now stand above the William Penn statue on City Hall, and together they block 18% of his horizon. Outside parks and public land, half of San Francisco is zoned for one or two family houses. In Philadelphia's most heat-vulnerable tracts, 98% of streets reach a park within ten minutes, but only 32% reach one of ten acres.

The Big Sur Marathon is drawn in plan and section with three line weights and one red line: the 510 ft climb to Hurricane Point. The Bombay map lays today's shoreline over the 1843 survey of the seven islands. New York's 314 Indian restaurants fall into 12 clusters.
Every map starts from the same Python toolkit, mapkit: the palettes, the credits and the title card live in one style file, and a publish script turns a finished notebook into a live page.
